population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. About 18% of US adults (~47M) are currently on an incretin for any reason. Roughly 10% of adults are former users currently off the drug, so the off-drug population that has been on it is now more than half the size of the on-drug population. Growth came through the cash tier (subscription orals at $149–299), Medicare's Part D obesity demonstration (65+ roughly doubled from 9% to 16%), diabetes/cardiac/OSA-coded coverage, and about 1.2M low-dose 'quiet' subscribers, most without obesity. Income gradient: the top third leads despite higher obesity in the bottom third. The bottom third depends on Medicaid in the ~16 states that cover obesity, on diabetes codes, or on gray-market supply. An estimated 3M users (~6% of users) take some unapproved product, mostly mail-order Indian or Chinese generic semaglutide and 'research' retatrutide. Persistence is still poor: ~38% of weight-management starters remain on therapy at one year. 46% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once, usually at a coverage loss, a price step or a GI episode. Pediatric: 12–17 use rose modestly under specialist care. Under-12 off-label prescribing fell by about two-thirds after 11 states barred it. The upper-income skew in teen prescribing persists (~1.6×). US adult obesity is estimated at ~33.5%, down from 36.4%.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the 2026 Bridge pilot rolled into CMS's Part D obesity demonstration (BALANCE) in January 2028. Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 copay where plans participate, so coverage is broad but not universal. The IRA negotiated price for semaglutide ($274) applies from 2027. Medicaid: ~16 states cover obesity at the federal rate. Several others dropped or never added coverage on budget grounds. Retatrutide is not yet in either programme's obesity coverage, pending its own price deal.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India $8–45/month and falling. Canada CAD 85–110. Chinese generics launched 2027 and are now the main low-cost exporter alongside India. Brazil and Mexico are generic markets. Generic semaglutide is available in ~170 countries. US exclusivity is unchanged (~2031–32). FDA has blocked bulk importation and warns against personal importation without seizing at scale.
access.note: The price path stalled. The scheduled cash step-down from ~$350 to $245 was paused in mid-2027 when Lilly and Novo invoked capacity provisions; HHS accepted in exchange for onshore manufacturing commitments. Cash prices: $299–349/month for injectable semaglutide and tirzepatide, $149 for oral starter doses rising to $249–299 at maintenance. Retatrutide lists at ~$1,399 with LillyDirect cash at ~$799, allocated by supply. Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 44% (FICTIONAL, BGH-style survey). Most remaining plans require a T2D, established CVD, OSA, MASH or CKD code, and payers now audit for 'coding drift'. The 503A/503B compounding exclusion is final. Demand that compounders used to serve has moved to mail-order foreign generics.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~30% of US households. Cumulative US volume decline since 2025 is ~4–6% in snacks and confectionery and ~3% in sugary drinks; total calorie demand is down ~2%. Protein, fibre and portion-tiered SKUs are standard. Marketing has split in two: 'right-sized' lines for on-drug households, and frank indulgence ('eat like you mean it') aimed at people who want to be seen hungry. Mid-tier snack brands are being consolidated. No major company has failed.

alcohol.state: US spirits and beer volumes keep falling (~3–4%/yr). Off-label AUD prescribing and 'quiet' plans, which users report dull the wish to drink, add to Gen Z moderation. Premium single-serve and non-alcoholic lines grow but do not offset the loss of heavy drinkers. Layoffs at mid-size distillers; Diageo and Brown-Forman are cutting brands.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. Casual-dining check sizes are down and mid-tier chains are squeezed. Small-plate and half-portion menus are standard, and the high end does well with 'appetite' tasting menus and steakhouses for diners performing hunger. Fast food is holding on value and on lower-income, less-medicated customers.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking, with store closures at Torrid-type chains. Mainstream brands have absorbed the smaller-size wave. Growth is in 'athletic' and muscle-fit cuts, tailoring and alterations, and size-fluid stretch lines for people who cycle.

fitness.state: Strength gyms, coaching and body-composition scanning are growing. Muscle has moved from preservation to display. Protein and creatine supplements are booming. A gray market in peptides and testosterone is growing in the muscle-ideal subculture.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is at 44%, and what remains is mostly coded to diabetes, cardiac, OSA or liver diagnoses with stiff prior authorisation and coding audits. Pharmacy trend is still high (~9–10%) because coded and Medicare volume keeps rising at flat prices. Some carriers sell standalone 'metabolic riders'. Two tiers are now formalised: coded patients pay copays, obesity-only patients pay cash.

pharma.state: Lilly holds ~60% of the US incretin market, helped by its orals and retatrutide. Novo is restructuring, defending semaglutide on price ex-US and losing share at home. US revenue grows on volume because prices are flat. Retatrutide is supply-allocated. Ex-US branded revenue is eroding to Indian and Chinese generics. Advertising restrictions have cut promotional spend and shifted it to physician detailing and direct-pay platforms.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A thin body now reads by default as medicated, so it no longer carries much status. Visible muscle, a big appetite and claimed 'unmedicated vitality' read as scarce, because they suggest time, money for trainers and food, and not needing the drug. Many people who display muscle are also on a pen; the claim is policed loosely and argued about constantly.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Partly inverted. Thinness no longer separates the top third from the middle, since cash-pay orals put it within reach of the middle class at $149–299/month. Muscle now does that work. The affluent quietly combine retatrutide with coaching, or perform being unmedicated. The bottom third has the highest obesity, the least coverage and the most gray-market use. Being heavy is still stigmatised, and is increasingly read as not being able to afford the pen rather than as a lack of willpower.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Mixed tables are normal: on-drug diners eat small plates beside performative eaters. Finishing a full plate in public has become a social signal. Some on-drug people eat bigger in public to look unmedicated. Family dinners where one partner is coded and covered and the other pays cash or abstains are a common domestic arrangement.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles commonly state 'unmedicated' or 'on reta' as an identity marker. Libido and connection complaints from on-drug partners are discussed openly in advice columns. Couples where only one partner is on the drug report mismatched appetites in food, drink and sex. None of this is quantified.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has split into two meanings. As craving, it is something to buy relief from: food noise, the evening drink, scrolling. As hunger, it is a sign of being alive and a status display. The same culture treats one as a defect and the other as vitality.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Uncontrolled 2027 surveys put reduced non-food enjoyment at 10–15% of users. Among ~1.2M 'quiet' subscribers it is the stated reason for use rather than a complaint. There are still no RCT measurements, and the effect remains 'emerging' in the ledger.
interior_life.framing: Feature, sold under names like 'quiet' and 'steady': calm, focus, freedom from craving. Medically it is still an unquantified side effect. Telehealth firms market it while avoiding explicit claims, and regulators police the marketing but not the use.
interior_life.effect_on_work: In sales, finance, call centres and tech, managers call on-drug staff 'unflappable'. Some workers say they start the drug to stop stress-snacking and doom-scrolling at their desks. A minority report lost ambition and quit side projects. Employers do not encourage use; most now drop coverage while informally liking the results.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Critics argue about 'flat' work. Some musicians and comedians lower or stop their dose before tours and say so publicly. 'Unmedicated' is a selling point in live music and stand-up. Intense-reward hobbies grow among users seeking to feel more: sour and spicy foods, extreme sports, loud venues.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Users report reduced desire and the feeling of being steady but distant. Partners describe the change as kinder and less present at once. Some couples time dose reductions around holidays. Not quantified.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect on turnout or polarisation. The drug has become a political object. 'Unmedicated' is a shared identity for MAHA-aligned populists and crunchy-left wellness culture, and both sides frame the 'quiet' market as pacification. Commentators speculate about calmer electorates without evidence.

state.regulatory_posture: Split. Federal regulators are pro-speed on approvals, with retatrutide approved under a priority voucher, while FDA, FTC and the states tightened promotion, telehealth and minors' access. The MAHA-led HHS treats incretin advertising and 'wellness' use as a problem even as it brokers access deals.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Medicare's Part D obesity demonstration (BALANCE) at ~$245 with a ~$50 copay where plans participate. Medicaid obesity coverage in ~16 states. The federal cash-price step-down was paused at $299–349. No subsidy for retatrutide.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Telehealth weight-management starts require a synchronous visit and documented BMI ≥27 with a comorbidity, or ≥30. Several states cap first prescriptions at a 90-day supply pending an in-person follow-up. Payer coding audits target 'drift' toward cardiac and OSA codes. 11 states bar under-12 prescribing and require a specialist, parental consent and registry enrolment for 12–17. There is no adherence surveillance beyond claims.
state.workforce_or_military: The Pentagon allows GLP-1 use to meet body-composition standards only through military treatment facilities. Recruits who used the drugs need a documented stable period before accession. Civilian employers make no requirements.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The price gap is now a fixed political fact: Toronto ~CAD 100 against Dayton $299+. China joined India as a generic exporter in 2027. The US blocks bulk importation and tolerates small parcels. Lilly and Novo traded the paused price cuts for onshore fill-finish capacity and tariff relief. Retatrutide is US-first and supply-constrained.

open_tensions: The two tiers have hardened. Diagnosis codes get a copay, obesity alone gets a stalled cash price or a mailed foreign generic, and retatrutide's surgical-grade loss goes first to those who can pay $799 a month or get onto an allocation list.

Calm is being sold as a product while the same effect is still logged as an unquantified side effect. Regulators have curbed the advertising but not the use, and no trial is designed to tell whether 'quiet' is relief or loss.

The muscle ideal is rising at the same moment the most effective drug strips the most lean mass. That pushes demand toward unapproved peptides, testosterone and muscle adjuncts that are still in trials.

The cycling population (46% of ever-users) and the 2026 teen cohort are growing up with no long-horizon data. New state restrictions limit new child starts but say nothing about the teenagers already on the drug.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: In 2028 the status body is muscled, hungry and proudly unmedicated, and you pay to stay calm
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 nearly one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, about 18 percent, and another one in ten has taken one and stopped. The drugs have become ordinary the way statins are ordinary, except that statins are covered. Employers kept retreating. Fewer than half still pay for weight management, and most of those have folded it into diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnoea codes. Access is now sorted by diagnosis. If your chart says type 2 diabetes or a prior heart attack, a pen arrives for a copay. If it says only obesity, you are in the cash tier. Prices there were supposed to keep sliding toward $245. Instead they have sat at $299 to $349 a month for injectables, and $149 to $299 for pills, since the manufacturers paused the step-down in mid-2027, citing demand and capacity. Medicare beneficiaries, under the Part D demonstration that took over from the 2026 bridge, are the cheapest customers in the country.

The growth came anyway: through pills bought on subscription, through Medicare, and through people who simply kept paying. It also came from a channel nobody planned for. Telehealth firms sell low-dose oral plans branded as quiet, promising calm, focus and freedom from craving, and they now count well over a million subscribers, many of them without obesity. No regulator has approved the drugs for anything like this; the alcohol trials are still in phase 3. The effect patients described in 2026 as feeling flat is now, in certain offices, described as being steady.

Washington pulls in two directions. The FDA cleared Lilly's retatrutide in December 2027 under a priority voucher, so a weekly pen now delivers close to 30 percent mean weight loss, the range that used to require surgery. Lilly rations it by supply and by a list price near $1,399, and bariatric surgeons report their first real dip in referrals. At the same time the agency, the FTC and a dozen state legislatures have closed doors. Broadcast and influencer advertising for these drugs is effectively over. Telehealth starts require a live visit and a documented BMI, and compounding is finished. Eleven states bar prescribing under twelve and require a specialist for teenagers. The restrictions bite hardest on the cash tier; the coded tier barely notices.

Mail fills the gap. Generic semaglutide costs under $50 a month in India and about a hundred Canadian dollars in Toronto, and Chinese manufacturers came online in 2027. Pens arrive in padded envelopes, and so-called research retatrutide is sold by the vial. Perhaps three million Americans use some unapproved supply.

The body has changed meaning. When thinness costs $149 a month, it stops saying much about anyone. A narrow waist now reads as medicated. What reads as expensive is muscle, which takes trainers, protein and time, and appetite, the visible pleasure of finishing a full plate. Unmedicated has become a boast on dating profiles and in casting calls. Wellness influencers, strength coaches and populist commentators use it with equal fervour, and plenty of the people photographed lifting are on a pen too. Gyms spent 2026 selling muscle preservation; now they sell muscle as display, and they are growing.

Food companies have stopped fighting. Snack and confectionery volumes keep easing and protein keeps climbing. Marketing is split between portion-tiered products for medicated households and frank indulgence for people who want to be seen hungry. Alcohol is still shrinking. Restaurants serve half plates at one table and tasting menus to performative eaters at the next.

Underneath, the population keeps cycling. Nearly half of those who have ever used the drugs have stopped and restarted at least once, usually when coverage, cash or patience ran out. Teenagers who started at thirteen are now fifteen. Nobody has data on either group beyond about six years. The ledger of known harms has not grown, which is reassuring or not depending on how long you think it takes to look.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renata Pruitt sets two alarms, one for work and one for Sunday's pill. It's Thursday. She checks the pharmacy app anyway. Refill: $299. She closes it.

At the hospital scheduling desk in Dayton, the new hire, Kyle, has a sticker on his water bottle, a small grey circle with the word quiet in lowercase. He doesn't snack. He doesn't look up when the phone lines stack. In the huddle the supervisor called him unflappable.

Lunch is in the break room. Marisol is on retatrutide through her husband's union plan. She eats four almonds and a protein yogurt and talks about her son's tuxedo fitting. Renata has the leftover lasagna and eats all of it. Nobody says anything. She notices that nobody says anything.

At three her daughter texts from school: a screenshot of a girl from her class, lifting, captioned natty, never pinned. Then: can we go to the specialist or not. Renata types we'll talk, deletes it, and types we'll talk.

Her sister in Toronto calls on the drive home. She's switched to the generic, ninety-four dollars. I could mail you some. Don't mail me anything.

Dinner. Darnell's pen lives in the butter compartment, because his A1c makes him a covered person. He used to have two beers on Thursdays. Now he has seltzer, asks how her day was, and listens carefully, the way he listens now.

After he's asleep she opens the app again. $299. The gym across from the Kroger has a banner: EAT. LIFT. FEEL IT. She thinks about the lasagna, how good it was, how hungry she's been all week. She doesn't hit refill. Not tonight.

population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. 15.2% of US adults are currently on an incretin drug for any reason (11% in 2026); 26% have ever used one. That leaves about 11% of adults as former users who are currently off, the largest group touched by the drugs that nobody counts as 'on'. Income is U-shaped, not a gradient. The bottom third (14.8%) was lifted by the January 2028 federal free-oral programme for Medicaid and uninsured adults. The top third (18.5%) was lifted by off-label 'metabolic health' and longevity use. The middle third (12.4%) is lowest: these are households whose employers dropped weight-loss coverage, who earn too much for Medicaid, and who were hit hardest by the 2027–28 injectable shortage and cash-price rise. Where the 4.2 pp came from: about +2.2 pp from public programmes (Medicaid model, the Medicare Bridge extension, health centres) and about +1.6 pp from wellness use by people without obesity or diabetes, who are now roughly 14% of current users, about 2.1% of adults. Cash and other routes added about +1.2 pp, and employer retreat took away about −0.8 pp. Roughly 1.0–1.2 million injectable users were displaced by the shortage. About half moved to oral drugs, about a fifth stopped (most of those visibly regained weight), and the rest went to compounders or imported generics. Among people who stopped, the restart pattern still holds (about 40% restart within a year), and 44% of ever-users have now stopped at least once and restarted. Under-18 use is 0.6%, mostly adolescents 12–17 after tirzepatide's adolescent approval in 2027. Prescribing still skews to upper-income families; Medicaid's free-oral model excludes minors. About 30% of US households now contain a current user, so a generation of children is eating at tables where adults finish half a plate. Adult obesity prevalence is about 34.8% (36.4% in 2026). Medicaid work requirements are disenrolling some adults mid-therapy, and their numbers are not tracked.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot was extended in December 2027 as a CMMI model through 2029 at the same ~$245 government price and $50 copay, $0 for Part D Low-Income Subsidy enrollees. Medicaid: from January 2028 a federally funded CMMI model in 34 states pays the full drug cost of daily oral GLP-1s (orforglipron and oral semaglutide), bulk-purchased at about $100/month, at $0 copay for adults with BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with a comorbidity). HRSA supplies the same pills free to uninsured patients through community health centres. Injectables and next-generation drugs are excluded from the free tier. The programme runs at about $5B/year annualised, on top of Medicare's spending. Federal employees (FEHB) retain anti-obesity coverage.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide sells in India ($6–40/month, including generic oral), Canada (~CAD 70–100), Brazil and China (patent expired 2026; dozens of domestic approvals and the main source of bulk API for the gray market), and is available in ~170 countries. US semaglutide exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32. A Florida-style Section 804 attempt to import Canadian generic semaglutide stalled after Canada's bulk-export restrictions.
access.note: The price shock: an FDA consent decree at a contract fill-finish site after sterility failures, plus a pen recall (Sept 2027), put several Wegovy/Ozempic pen strengths on the FDA shortage list until April 2028. Novo suspended new cash-channel injectable starts and paused discount programmes. Effective cash prices for injectables rose from ~$349 to ~$449–499, and Lilly raised higher-dose Zepbound vial pricing as demand shifted to it. The introductory $149 oral cash tier expired for new patients in January 2028, so the cash floor is now ~$199. The median out-of-pocket for cash payers is up about 35% in two years. The list-price ceiling ($1,499) is retatrutide and MariTide. The shortage listing legally reopened 503A/503B compounding of the listed strengths, undoing two years of FDA enforcement until the delisting. Personal importation of Canadian and Indian generics by mail and Chinese 'research peptide' vials (including unapproved retatrutide copies) fill the gap for the middle. Employers that dropped coverage increasingly offer 'navigation' benefits instead: access to a negotiated cash price with no coverage. The route mix keeps shifting: orals are about 40% of new starts, driven by the free-oral tier and fill-finish fragility.

drugs.pipeline_note: Amycretin is in phase 3 (readouts 2029). Implants (six-month subdermal GLP-1 devices) are in phase 1/2, years away. Muscle-preserving adjuncts (bimagrumab combinations) are in phase 3. Oral amylin and oral next-gen small molecules are in phase 2/3. MariTide's early uptake is limited by supply and by initiation vomiting at the first dose. The industry pitches it to employers and Medicaid plans as clinic-administered under the medical benefit, with adherence verifiable by administration record. The global incretin market is about $115B in 2028 and on track for $150B+ by 2030–31. Lilly holds about 60% of US new starts, and Novo has lost share to the shortage, the scandal and its weaker efficacy position.

Whether gastroparesis persists after stopping is disputed. MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) passed 20,000 filed cases in 2028, with tens of thousands more under tolling agreements and coordinated state-court dockets. Plaintiff advertising is national.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class labelling update (2028) strengthens ileus/obstruction warnings and perioperative aspiration guidance. A September 2028 Daubert ruling admitted general-causation experts on ileus and obstruction but narrowed claims of persistent gastroparesis to those with objective gastric-emptying studies. Bellwether trials are set for 2029.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss, and more visible with retatrutide-scale losses.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Long-term RCTs still do not confirm causation, and absolute risk is low. Pancreatitis claims are a large minority of the MDL docket. Pharmacogenetic susceptibility studies are ongoing.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled. Litigated at mass-tort scale.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–40% of weight lost is lean mass, worse at triple-agonist magnitudes and in older adults. Wellness users with normal BMI lose proportionally more lean mass. The bone-density signal persists.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. Guidance from professional societies recommends resistance training and protein targets. Muscle-preserving combinations are in phase 3.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict, and absolute risk is very low. A separate litigation track exists.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added 'very rare' NAION language to US semaglutide labels in 2027, matching the EMA.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association across EMA, MHRA and systematic reviews. Some users conflate it with the blunting question.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed (2026); not reinstated.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Labelled frequency is 'uncommon'. A 2028 Nordic registry analysis puts clinically significant anhedonia at about 1–2% of users, higher at top doses and with the triple agonist; about 7% self-report 'less enjoyment' in surveys. Most cases resolve with dose reduction. The 2027 unsealed documents showed a manufacturer patient-support survey had captured these reports without submitting them as adverse events.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA requested class labelling (Feb 2028): emotional blunting / loss of interest or pleasure, uncommon. Many obesity clinics now give a brief pleasure-scale questionnaire (SHAPS-style) at titration visits.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2027–28 shortage acted as an unplanned discontinuation experiment: forced stoppers regained about half of lost weight within 9 months in claims-linked data, a figure between the trial results and earlier real-world estimates.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. Reinforces chronic-therapy framing and payer interest in monthly, clinic-administered dosing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Concern has widened to normal-BMI wellness users on low intake. Protein and B12/iron shortfalls are reported in clinic series.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None formal. Society guidance recommends dietitian review.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist. Cycling is the norm (44% of ever-users). The shortage added an involuntary cycling cohort. No adolescent data beyond about 3 years.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on retatrutide and MariTide include long-term registries.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Resurged during the shortage: compounding reopened legally for listed strengths, counterfeit pens were seized at ports, and 'research peptide' vials of unapproved retatrutide circulated. Adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed 3,500.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The 503B bulks exclusion was finalised in 2027, but the shortage-list exemption overrode it until April 2028 delisting. CBP and FDA import alerts target Chinese API. Warning-letter waves resumed after delisting.

safety_ledger.effect: Harms of use in people without obesity (excess lean-mass loss, undernutrition, masking or triggering of eating disorders)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Concentrated in wellness and longevity use, about 2% of adults. Eating-disorder clinicians report GLP-1 use in a rising share of new adolescent and young-adult referrals. Not quantified nationally.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA warning letters to telehealth 'metabolic optimisation' advertisers for off-label promotion. Professional guidance against use below BMI 25 without comorbidity. No prescribing restriction.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen in phase 3 and in early post-launch reports; mostly mild and transient.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled at approval (Mar 2028).

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are about 30% of US households. Snack, confectionery and sugary-drink volumes decline 1–3% a year, and several snack-plant consolidations have been announced. Protein, fibre and 'metabolic' claims cover the shelf. Wellness users skew premium, so 'longevity' SKUs (high-protein, small-format, functional) grow while value multipacks shrink. Revenue is defended by price-per-ounce increases on smaller packs.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down for a third straight year and beer keeps sliding. Heavy-drinker downshift is now visible in distributor data. Non-alcoholic and low-ABV products grow but do not replace margin. The industry lobbies quietly against AUD-indication marketing, and its trade groups argue the off-label AUD prescribing wave lacks phase 3 support.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. 'Half-portion' and small-plate menus are standard at casual and fine dining. Average check is held by premiumisation, but alcohol attach rates have fallen, squeezing bar margins and the tipped staff who depended on them.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking through store closures and range cuts. Mainstream apparel benefits from re-sizing waves. The shortage briefly reversed this as forced stoppers re-bought up. Tailoring and alteration services grow.

fitness.state: Strength training, body-composition scanning (DEXA bars) and 'muscle insurance' programmes are the fastest-growing segment. Gyms partner with telehealth wellness prescribers. Muscle has become the visible marker of doing the drug well.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is at 44% (60% in 2026). Coverage concentrates on diabetes, cardiovascular, sleep-apnea, MASH and kidney codes, so diagnosis now decides benefit. Cash-price navigation stipends replace coverage at many firms. Pharmacy trend is moderating for employers that dropped coverage while public spending grows. Medicaid plans and some employers are piloting MariTide under the medical benefit with administration-record adherence.

pharma.state: Lilly is dominant on efficacy (retatrutide) and orals. Novo is hit by the fill-finish failure, the pharmacovigilance warning letter and the litigation; its shares fell about 20% across 2027. Amgen enters with the first monthly drug. The free-oral bulk contract at ~$100/month resets price expectations for orals, so revenue grows on volume while unit prices fall everywhere except new launches.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it is unremarkable; being visibly off it gets asked about. The 2027 shortage made regain public, and 'did you get cut off?' became a recognisable question. In affluent and middle-aged circles an unmedicated heavier body is read as a choice that needs explaining: cost, side effects, conviction, or pregnancy.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Free orals at the bottom have weakened thinness as a class marker. Class now shows in which drug and how you got it: monthly or triple-agonist injectables with a coach and DEXA scans at the top, free daily pills at the bottom, mailed imported vials in the middle. Visible muscle and 'good composition' are the new tell of money.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared plates and half portions are the norm. Hosts plan for guests eating little. Holiday meals shrink in volume but not in ceremony. Children in about 30% of households grow up with adults who eat lightly by default, and pediatricians report parents asking when their children can start.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Medication status is discussed early on dates, like drinking habits. Mismatch (one partner on, one off) is a common couples-therapy theme: diverging appetites for food, drink and late nights. The labelled libido and blunting effects give couples a vocabulary but remain a minority experience.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a dial a clinician can set, and for wellness users as something to optimise even without disease. Wanting a second helping reads to some as a symptom. A counter-current, including fat-acceptance and 'unmedicated' food culture, frames appetite as a pleasure worth keeping.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Since February 2028 class labelling lists emotional blunting / loss of interest or pleasure as uncommon. Registry estimates put clinically significant cases at about 1–2% of users, and about 7% self-report some loss of enjoyment. Effects are dose-related and more frequent on the triple agonist, and most resolve with dose reduction. Clinics screen at titration. With 15% of adults on a drug, an 'uncommon' effect still means something like half a million to a million people.
interior_life.framing: A labelled, dose-dependent side effect, managed like nausea: you report it and the dose comes down. Patients call it 'going flat'. The same mechanism is still pursued as AUD treatment in phase 3, and some wellness users describe the quieting of craving as the point. Clinicians separate the two by dose and by whether pleasure in non-food life is lost.
interior_life.effect_on_work: No measurable productivity effect in employer data. Anecdotes run both ways: quieter craving and fewer afternoon slumps, versus some users describing diminished ambition. Employers do not encourage or monitor use. Occupational health asks about it only for safety-sensitive roles.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Bar and late-night venue spending is down more than attendance. Comedians and TV writers use 'going flat' as a stock joke. A minority of musicians and chefs publicly refuse the drug or take 'creative holidays' from it. Intense-flavour foods (sour, spicy, bitter) remain a marketing category built on blunted users chasing sensation.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Decreased libido and emotional distance are listed effects for some. Relationship counsellors report the on/off mismatch more often than blunting itself. Dose reduction is a common couples' negotiation.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No observable effect of blunting on political behaviour. The drug itself is political: free pills for Medicaid, the squeezed middle, the scandal, and 'MAHA' diet-first rhetoric coexisting uneasily with an administration that buys the pills.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-speed on approvals (retatrutide and MariTide under priority review). Tougher on pharmacovigilance after the 2027 scandal: a warning letter, class labelling and a request for psychiatric-adverse-event capture in patient-support programmes. Enforcement against compounders and off-label wellness advertising, undercut by the shortage-list exemption during 2027–28.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy without mandate. The Medicare Bridge was extended through 2029 (~$245 price, $50 or $0 copay). Federally funded free oral GLP-1s run through a CMMI Medicaid model in 34 states and HRSA health centres for the uninsured, bulk-bought at ~$100/month, costing ~$5B/year annualised. Pills only; injectables are excluded.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The free tier requires annual BMI/A1c documentation and a single nutrition-counselling visit. Medicaid work requirements (in force from 2027) disenroll adults mid-therapy with no continuity provision. Monthly MariTide pilots under the medical benefit create administration-record adherence data, which payers are beginning to discuss as a renewal condition. No mandate or benefit penalty yet.
state.workforce_or_military: The Army is piloting supervised pre-accession GLP-1 use to bring otherwise-eligible applicants within body-fat standards; recruits must be off-drug at shipping. FEHB keeps anti-obesity coverage, making federal and public-sector jobs a quiet access advantage. The FAA permits pilots on stable doses with conditions.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The fill-finish failure exposed how concentrated US sterile manufacturing is and pushed policy toward small-molecule orals. Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs exempt firms with US capital pledges, and Lilly and Novo traded the bulk-oral price for relief. Chinese generic semaglutide API is the backbone of the gray market and a CBP enforcement target. Canada restricts bulk exports, blocking state importation schemes. The US–rest-of-world price gap ($199+ vs $6–40) is an election-year talking point.

events.event: Documents unsealed in the federal GLP-1 gastrointestinal MDL show Novo Nordisk safety staff labelled a 2020–21 intestinal-obstruction signal 'non-actionable' and that a company patient-support survey captured reports of lost enjoyment that were never filed as adverse events. Novo says it met reporting rules. FDA issues a pharmacovigilance warning letter, and its chief safety officer departs.

A contract fill-finish site making semaglutide pens enters an FDA consent decree after sterility failures and a lot recall. FDA lists several Wegovy and Ozempic pen strengths in shortage. Novo halts new cash-channel injectable starts, and effective cash prices for injectables rise about a third. Compounding of the listed strengths becomes legal again.

As the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge is extended through 2029, HHS launches free oral GLP-1 pills for Medicaid adults with obesity in 34 states and for uninsured patients at community health centres, bought in bulk at about $100 a month from Lilly and Novo.

Gallup puts current US adult incretin use at 15%, with about one in seven users reporting neither obesity nor diabetes and citing 'metabolic health' or longevity. Business Group on Health finds only 44% of large employers still cover weight management, with coverage concentrated on diabetes and cardiac codes.

The GLP-1 MDL passes 20,000 filed cases. The judge admits plaintiffs' causation experts on ileus and bowel obstruction but limits gastroparesis claims to patients with objective gastric-emptying tests. Bellwether trials are set for 2029.

FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly obesity injection. Initial supply is limited, and Medicaid plans and large employers begin piloting it as a clinic-administered drug under the medical benefit.

open_tensions: The access system is three tiers: free daily pills for the poor, gray-market vials for the middle, and monthly or triple-agonist injectables for the covered and the rich. Medicaid work requirements eject people from the free tier mid-therapy. The programme's ~$5B line item depends on whichever administration takes office in January 2029.

About 2% of adults with no disease are now taking drugs whose labels list ileus, obstruction and emotional blunting, under a manufacturer that hid signals once and in litigation bellwethers due in 2029. No trial has tested benefit in the healthy, and no one has decided who carries the liability.

Monthly clinic-administered dosing ends the weekly choice and creates the first reliable adherence records. Payers are already discussing tying renewal to them. Meanwhile the shortage forced a new involuntary cycling cohort onto a population whose decade-long on/off trajectory is unstudied.

Blunting is a labelled side effect and also, at different doses, the treatment target in AUD phase 3 and the selling point for wellness users. It is still unsettled whether a quieted appetite for pleasure is harm, therapy or product.

prose.headline: Free Pills for the Poor, Monthly Shots for the Rich, Mailed Vials for Everyone Else: America at 15%
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028, about one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, and roughly one in four has been at some point. The number nobody headlines is the gap between the two. About a tenth of the adult population used to be on one and is now off, some by choice and many not. In most offices, at most dinner tables and on most first dates, being on the drug no longer draws comment. What draws a second look is a body that has visibly put weight back on, because since the autumn of 2027 people have known what that usually means.

What it usually meant was the shortage. A contract plant that filled semaglutide pens failed sterility inspections, signed a consent decree and recalled lots. For seven months several pen strengths sat on the FDA shortage list. Novo stopped taking new cash patients for injectables, and the effective price of a month's supply rose by about a third. Then a quirk of the law did what two years of warning letters had tried to prevent: the shortage listing made compounding legal again. The middle of the market went back to vials, from pharmacies, from Canadian and Indian mail-order sites, and from Chinese peptide sellers who label their product 'not for human use'. The shortage ended in April and the enforcement resumed, but the habit stayed.

The squeezed middle is the system's defining feature. Employers kept retreating, and fewer than half of large firms now cover weight management. What survives is coverage written to diagnosis codes: diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnoea, liver and kidney. Many firms that dropped coverage offer a 'navigation' benefit instead, which is a link to a negotiated cash price. Below that middle, Washington did something few predicted. In January 2028 it began buying daily oral pills in bulk at about a hundred dollars a month and giving them free to Medicaid adults in 34 states and to uninsured patients at community health centres. Medicare's bridge pilot was extended to 2029. The poorest third is now more likely to be on a drug than the middle third, though work requirements remove some of them from Medicaid in mid-treatment and nobody counts what happens to them next.

At the top, the drugs have left the clinic for the wellness market. About one user in seven has neither obesity nor diabetes and takes a low dose for 'metabolic health', bundled by telehealth firms with blood panels, DEXA scans and a coach. No trial has tested the benefit in healthy people. Muscle has become the visible marker of money: anyone can be thin now, but a lean, strong body suggests a trainer and the newest molecule. Lilly's triple agonist, retatrutide, has been on sale since March. Amgen's monthly injection was approved in October and is being piloted as a clinic-administered drug, which gives payers their first reliable adherence records.

The ledger has grown heavier. Documents unsealed in 2027 showed Novo safety staff had marked an old bowel-obstruction signal 'non-actionable' and had collected patient reports of lost enjoyment without filing them as adverse events. The federal litigation has passed twenty thousand cases, and bellwether trials begin next year. Emotional blunting is now on the label as uncommon, and clinics screen for it at titration the way they ask about nausea. The same blunting effect is the target of an alcohol-use-disorder trial, and some wellness clients cite it as the reason they take the drug.

On the surface, things look orderly. Obesity is down, holiday meals are smaller, bar tabs are lighter, and plus-size shops are closing quietly. Who pays, for whom, and for how long is still unresolved, and the answer depends on the next budget and on who takes office in January.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Ochoa wakes at 5:40 in Toledo and takes the vial out of the butter compartment. The label is in English and French. She draws twenty units in the bathroom so the kids don't watch, pinches her stomach and counts to six.

At the plant's payroll office the break-room fridge is full of small yogurts. Denise from receiving holds up a white pharmacy bag: "Free. Health center." She shakes it like a maraca. Marisol earns eleven hundred dollars a year too much for that bag. She knows the exact figure.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and rewraps the rest for tomorrow. Her phone shows a law-firm ad: Did you suffer bowel obstruction? She swipes it away. A second ad: Longevity, optimized. A woman with arms like cables.

At pickup her son Nico, nine, asks why Tía Lupe got fat again. "She didn't get fat," Marisol says. "Her pen ran out." Nico nods. That makes sense to him.

Dinner is chicken thighs and rice. Her husband Ray, who isn't on anything, takes seconds. Then he looks at her plate and puts the spoon back, and she wishes he hadn't.

After the kids are in bed she checks the order page. The Canadian site now says shipments are delayed at customs. There is a cheaper listing from somewhere else, with a lab report, a crisp PDF.

She puts on the old cumbia playlist from her wedding and waits to feel it. Mostly she does. She turns it up a little anyway.

population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. Survey data from late 2028 put about 21% of US adults currently on an incretin for any reason. About 32% have ever used one. So roughly 1 adult in 9 is a former user who is currently off. Persistence has improved but cycling is still the norm. One-year persistence among weight-management starters rose from ~35% to ~46%, mostly because cost-driven stopping fell once unbranded semaglutide hit $59. About 44% of ever-users have stopped at least once and restarted. The income gradient has narrowed but not closed. Medicaid coverage and $0 provision at community health centres pulled the bottom third up from an estimated ~6% to ~18%. The lowest-use group is now the band between subsidy eligibility and good coverage: working adults at 200–350% of the poverty line in plans that dropped coverage. They show the highest stop-start rates. Medicaid work requirements, in force from 2027, add churn: an estimated 1 in 7 Medicaid users had a coverage gap of 60+ days in 2028. The top third includes a growing group without obesity. Roughly 3–4% of all adults, mostly affluent, take low 'metabolic health', longevity or 'calm' doses, often outside insurance and partly through the gray market. 65+ use roughly doubled under the extended Medicare bridge. Under-18 use is ~1.2% overall, mostly adolescents 12–17 with obesity, still skewed to the insured. About 4 in 10 US children now live in a household with at least one current user. US adult obesity prevalence is estimated at ~33%, down from 36.4%.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge demonstration was extended through Dec 2028 rather than allowed to lapse. In Dec 2027 Congress lifted the statutory Part D exclusion of weight-loss drugs, effective Jan 2029. It passed after CBO cut its score by more than half once unbranded semaglutide repriced the market. Medicare pays ~$245 for branded tirzepatide/semaglutide under the 2025 deals and the 2027 negotiated price. The preferred tier is unbranded semaglutide at ~$70, with a $0–10 copay. Medicaid: ~38 state programs cover unbranded semaglutide for obesity, most at $0 copay. Several others cover it only under the alcohol-use-disorder pathway. A federal HRSA grant line (the 'Metabolic Health Access' program) provides unbranded semaglutide free at community health centres to uninsured adults under 200% FPL, conditional on a nutrition-visit enrollment. Public programs now pay for a majority of new starts.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide is sold in ~160 countries. India: ~$5–30/month, 60+ brands. China: multiple domestic generics since its 2026 patent lapse, and a major peptide-API exporter. Canada: CAD 60–90/month. Brazil and Mexico: generic and local brands. EU, UK and Japan remain brand-only until ~2031. Personal-import mail-order from India and Canada reaches US consumers at $15–40/month.
access.note: US price collapse runs through near-generics, not legal generics. Semaglutide and tirzepatide exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32. In Aug 2027, Novo Nordisk launched an unbranded semaglutide (injectable pens, cash $59/month) under its own label. The playbook matches insulin's authorised generics, aimed at undercutting imports and holding volume. Lilly cut Foundayo starter doses to $79 and higher doses to $99–129. Generic liraglutide (daily, ~5–8% loss) sells at $39–60. Premium tiers remain: retatrutide (approved 2028) lists at ~$1,499 with ~$499 cash via the manufacturer, and MariTide (monthly, approved Oct 2028) lists at ~$1,249. Employers cite the $59 sticker as the reason for dropping coverage; many now offer an HSA stipend instead. Gray market: FDA tolerates personal importation under 90-day enforcement discretion. At the same time CBP seizures of counterfeit pens rose roughly 9× between 2026 and 2028. Non-prescription 'wellness' demand from people ineligible for coverage is the gray market's core customer base. Weekly injectables are ~58% of volume, daily orals ~40%, monthly <2% at year end.

GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026; modest uptake after failing non-inferiority vs tirzepatide)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028)
GLP-1 agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide, approved Oct 2028)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 small-molecule, daily oral (orforglipron: Foundayo)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: adolescent obesity 12+ (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide label expansion 2027)

alcohol use disorder — guideline-endorsed, not yet FDA-approved: ASAM and VA/DoD (Nov 2027) list semaglutide as a second-line pharmacotherapy for AUD, first-line where obesity co-occurs; pivotal-trial readout and sNDA expected 2029
mainstream_offlabel_uses: low-dose 'metabolic health' and longevity use by people without obesity: telehealth subscriptions, concierge medicine and gray-market pens; est. 3–4% of US adults
'calm / focus / freedom from craving' plans: low-dose semaglutide or Foundayo marketed by telehealth wellness brands for food noise, phone and shopping compulsions, and work focus
alcohol reduction in people without diagnosed AUD ('dry-curious' prescribing)
nicotine and vaping cessation: observational support, trials ongoing
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care, still rare
drugs.pipeline_note: Retatrutide's label carries dysesthesia and higher GI discontinuation. Uptake is concentrated in cash-pay and premium commercial plans. MariTide's monthly dosing is pitched to payers as an adherence fix, but it is barely in pharmacies at year end. Amycretin (injectable and oral) is in phase 3 with readouts 2029. Survodutide filed for MASH and obesity. Bimagrumab plus semaglutide (muscle preservation) is in phase 3 and marketed as the upcoming answer to lean-mass loss. No implant has reached filing. Analyst 2030 global incretin revenue forecasts fell from $150–162B to ~$115–130B even as volume forecasts rose: price per patient fell faster than patients grew. Novo announced a second restructuring (Mar 2028). Lilly's revenue keeps growing on tirzepatide, orforglipron and retatrutide.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and leading cause of discontinuation. Higher with retatrutide. Dosing errors with imported and counterfeit product add GI hospitalisations.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; gastroparesis caution retained.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss. Cholecystectomy volume up measurably in Medicare claims since the bridge pilot.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal confirmation in long-term RCTs. Absolute risk low. Case reports cluster with counterfeit and overdosed product.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; mass-tort litigation consolidated, unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Medicare observational data from the bridge cohort show a small rise in fall-related fractures among users over 75 who lost >15% of body weight. Effect sizes are disputed and confounded. Concern is concentrated in older adults and repeated cyclers, who regain mostly fat.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. Several Medicare contractors recommend resistance-training and protein counselling at initiation. Muscle-sparing adjuncts are in phase 3.

safety_ledger.effect: NAION (non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) / sudden optic-nerve vision loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A pooled FDA Sentinel and multinational cohort analysis (2026–27) found a consistent ~1.7–2× relative risk across GLP-1 receptor agonists. Baseline incidence is low (~2–10 per 100,000 per year), so excess risk is on the order of a few extra cases per 100,000 users per year. At US scale that means thousands of additional cases annually. Risk is higher in people with diabetes, a 'crowded' optic disc, or prior NAION in one eye.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class-wide Warnings and Precautions label (Feb 2027) for all GLP-1 receptor agonist products, with patient Medication Guide language on sudden vision loss. Ophthalmology societies advise baseline eye exams for high-risk patients. Products liability filings rose sharply.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association in EMA, MHRA and FDA reviews. Larger datasets since 2026 have not reopened it.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed (2026). Gray-market product carries no labelling at all.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: First quantified in 2027–28. A large patient-reported cohort using validated anhedonia scales found clinically meaningful score increases in ~9% of users vs ~5% of matched non-users, dose-related and mostly reversible on dose reduction. A secondary analysis of an AUD trial found reduced reward response to non-drug cues as well as alcohol. The effect is now both a reported harm and a marketed benefit.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. FDA requested anhedonia measures in postmarketing studies for new approvals. FTC warning letters (2028) to three telehealth brands over unsubstantiated 'focus' and 'calm' claims.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Real-world data converge between trial and claims estimates. Roughly half to two-thirds of lost weight returns within 12–18 months of stopping. Coverage-gap cyclers show repeated regain.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. Drives chronic-therapy framing. Medicaid continuity-of-care rules are debated.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Case series of thiamine, B12 and iron deficiency in users eating very little, especially older adults and people on low-dose wellness plans with restrictive diets.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: HRSA program requires a nutrition visit. No label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescent use over decades; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of RCT follow-up now exists. No signal beyond known effects, and no data on cycling or adolescent-to-adult use.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals. NIH funded a 10-year pediatric registry (2027).

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded, imported and counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination, wrong active ingredient)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Over 5,000 FDA adverse-event reports by 2028. A 2027 CDC health alert linked 312 emergency visits in 14 states to counterfeit pens, some containing insulin (severe hypoglycaemia), with two deaths. Endotoxin-contaminated vials and 2–10× concentration errors are recurrent.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised (2027). CBP and FDA import operations, with seizures up ~9× since 2026. Personal importation is still tolerated, a policy contradiction FDA has not resolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen in phase 3, mostly mild and transient, more common at higher doses.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled at retatrutide approval (Apr 2028).

safety_ledger.effect: Low-dose use in people without obesity (longevity / 'calm' plans)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No RCTs in lean or normal-weight populations. Benefit claims rest on extrapolation, while lean-mass and micronutrient risks may be proportionally larger.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None specific. Off-label prescribing is legal. FTC acts on advertising, not use.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~36% of US households. Cumulative packaged-snack and confectionery volume is down ~7% since 2024, and sugary carbonated drinks down ~5%. Revenue losses are partly offset by price per unit, protein reformulation and mini formats. Two large snack makers divested legacy brands. Plant consolidations cut several thousand manufacturing jobs, concentrated in the Midwest and South. Private label gains as smaller baskets trade down. 'Protein per calorie' is the dominant claim on shelf.

alcohol.state: US spirits volume down ~4% a year in 2027–28 and beer down faster. Heavy-drinker trading-down, now reinforced by the AUD guideline and a plausible on-label approval in 2029, hits the top-decile drinkers who carry the category. Distillers pivot to premium small formats, low-ABV and ready-to-drink. Craft brewery closures accelerate, and distributors consolidate.

restaurants.state: Traffic roughly flat overall, but all-you-can-eat and value-heavy casual dining lose traffic. Half-portion and 'small plate at full price' menus are standard. Average check holds via premium proteins and one 'occasion' cocktail. Drink attachment rates are falling. Delivery order sizes are shrinking.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting, with store closures and one chain restructuring. The mainstream re-buy wave at smaller sizes has largely passed. Alterations and tailoring see a small boom. Fitted, muscle-showing cuts and performance wear lead growth in upper-income segments.

fitness.state: Strength training, coached small-group and 'lean-mass' programmes grow fastest, with DEXA body-composition scans as an upscale add-on. Budget gyms are flat. Premium strength studios and in-home coaching are the growth, priced well above what the $59 user can spend.

insurance.state: Commercial plans and employers retreat to 44% coverage and point members to cash at $59. Some offer HSA stipends. Pharmacy trend moderates as unit cost falls. Medicare and Medicaid absorb volume. Part D plans prepare premium increases for the 2029 exclusion lift. Prior-auth fights shift to the premium agents (retatrutide, MariTide).

pharma.state: Volume is up sharply and price per patient sharply down. Novo is in a second restructuring after cannibalising its own brand with unbranded semaglutide. Lilly leads on tirzepatide, oral orforglipron and retatrutide. Amgen enters with monthly dosing. Indian and Chinese generic makers win the rest of the world and supply the US gray market indirectly. 2030 revenue forecasts revised down.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness no longer signals money because it costs $59 or is free at the health centre. What it signals now is which drug, how much muscle, and how the weight came off. A lean body with visible shoulders and arms, even skin, and steady weight reads as premium agents, coaching, protein and time. A thin-soft body, a face that lost volume fast, or a body visibly between regain and loss reads as generic, cycling or gray market. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured, rural or deliberate.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Body shape has become an income proxy, but the gradient moved: access is almost universal, while quality, continuity and muscle are not. Generic-semaglutide users in the coverage gap cycle with their finances. Affluent users stay continuous on retatrutide, add strength coaching and enter trials for muscle-sparing adjuncts. Lean affluent people take low 'longevity' doses they don't medically need. A visible minority rejects the drugs as identity: body-neutral activists, some religious communities, some athletes. 'Never-on' is a claim of authenticity in some circles and an admission of poverty in others.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are smaller and shorter. Holiday tables plan for half the food. Families have mixed appetites at one table, with children often the only ones finishing plates. Snacking as social glue has thinned at offices and schools. Restaurants sell 'the occasion' rather than the volume. In households where adults are on-drug, children's food environments are shrinking too: fewer snacks bought, fewer family dinners cooked at scale. Pediatricians are watching for under-eating and over-eating.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles commonly state 'on', 'off' or 'never', and some apps added filters in 2028. Alcohol-free first dates are normal among under-40s. Couples therapists describe 'appetite mismatch': one partner on-drug and calm, the other not, with a shared life built around food and drink coming apart. Reduced libido is reported often enough to be a dinner-party topic. Low-dose 'calm' users are sometimes described by partners as easier and more distant at once.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite of any kind is now widely treated as an adjustable setting rather than a trait. Craving for food, drink, scrolling or shopping is something one can dial down for $59 a month. Wanting a lot is quietly coded as either unmedicated or chosen.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: First quantified in 2027–28. Roughly 9% of users report clinically meaningful anhedonia increases vs ~5% of matched non-users. The effect is dose-related and mostly reversible. Separately, a large and unmeasured share of low-dose users take the drug for this effect: telehealth brands sell 'quiet' and 'calm' subscriptions to people without obesity, for food noise, alcohol, phone use and focus. The clinic calls it a side effect, the AUD guideline calls it a mechanism, and the wellness market calls it the product.
interior_life.framing: Feature, in the market. Telehealth and wellness brands sell craving-free calm and focus. Manufacturers stay silent because off-label promotion is illegal for them. In clinics it is still a side effect to dose-adjust, and in addiction medicine it is a treatment. FTC warning letters target specific claims without disturbing the category.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Low-dose 'focus' plans are popular among knowledge workers, traders and some sales staff, bought privately. No employer formally encourages them, but a few tech and finance firms' wellness stipends can be spent on them. Managers report fewer after-work drinks and flatter client dinners, and sales and hospitality veterans complain the 'entertaining' economy is quieter. An early working paper linking claims to payroll data finds no detectable earnings or productivity effect in either direction. Anecdotes of lost ambition and of newfound steadiness remain about equally common.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Nightlife has shifted toward earlier, shorter, lower-alcohol evenings. Intensity products are selling: extreme sour, heat, loud live shows, cold plunges, ultra-endurance events. Some explain this as users chasing a signal that registers. Being off-drug has become a minor credential among musicians, comedians and chefs, and 'unmedicated appetite' is a marketing line for some restaurants. Stand-up and TV satire about 'quiet' partners and silent dinner parties is a recognisable genre. Sports-betting and mobile-game firms note small engagement declines among on-drug cohorts in their own data and do not discuss them publicly.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire is commonly reported. Partners of low-dose 'calm' users describe them as easier to live with and harder to reach. Some couples synchronise, both on or both off. Mixed couples report friction around food, drink and spontaneity. Clinicians increasingly advise dose reduction rather than stopping when libido complaints arise.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect on turnout or partisanship has been shown. The idea that it might exist is itself a political force: populist voices on both the right and the left call the free HRSA provision and Medicaid coverage 'sedating the poor'. Some MAHA-aligned figures attack the program their own administration expanded. Alcohol, snack and sugar-state lobbies quietly fund some of that messaging. Campaigns test 'calm voter' targeting theories that nobody can verify.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and fast on approvals: retatrutide in a standard cycle, MariTide under a priority voucher. Safety labelling is firmer: a class NAION warning in 2027. Enforcement on supply is contradictory: aggressive against compounders and counterfeiters, tolerant of personal importation of foreign generics, and largely hands-off on off-label low-dose prescribing apart from FTC advertising actions.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy and free provision with no mandate. Free unbranded semaglutide at community health centres for uninsured adults under 200% FPL (HRSA grant line, launched Jan 2028). $0–10 copays in most Medicaid programs and the extended Medicare bridge. Part D exclusion lifted effective 2029. Federal incretin spending is estimated at ~$14B in 2028, far below 2025 projections per patient because unit prices collapsed.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The HRSA program requires a nutrition-visit enrollment and a 6-month weight and refill check to continue. Medicaid coverage is subject to 2027 work-requirement reporting, so missed reports interrupt therapy and produce state-induced cycling. Pharmacy refill data drive continuation decisions in Medicare. No biometric monitoring of off-label or cash users.
state.workforce_or_military: DoD accession guidance (2027) allows waivers for applicants who met body-composition standards on a GLP-1 and remain stable on it, and recruiters cite the policy in markets with high obesity. No mandates on service members or civilian workers.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: India and China dominate generic supply worldwide and indirectly feed the US gray market. China is also the main source of peptide API in counterfeits. US exclusivity to ~2031–32 now protects brands mainly in the US premium tier. Novo's and Lilly's US manufacturing investments are traded for tariff relief. The visible US–abroad price gap has narrowed from ~40× to ~2–4× for semaglutide.

events.event: FDA adds a class-wide Warnings and Precautions label for sudden optic-nerve vision loss (NAION) to all GLP-1 receptor agonists, citing a pooled Sentinel and international cohort analysis showing roughly doubled relative risk.

CDC health alert links 312 emergency visits in 14 states, and two deaths, to counterfeit and mislabeled imported semaglutide pens, some found to contain insulin; CBP announces a surge in mail-facility seizures.
Novo Nordisk launches unbranded semaglutide pens at $59 a month cash, undercutting personal imports; Lilly cuts Foundayo starter doses to $79 within three weeks.
ASAM and VA/DoD guidelines endorse semaglutide for alcohol use disorder; within weeks, major telehealth platforms roll out low-dose 'calm' and 'focus' subscriptions for people without obesity.

Congress lifts the Part D exclusion on weight-loss drugs effective 2029 and extends the Medicare GLP-1 bridge through 2028; HHS announces free unbranded semaglutide at community health centres for uninsured adults under 200% of poverty from January.
FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly obesity injection, at a $1,249 list price; payers call it an adherence fix and place it on the highest tier.

open_tensions: Access is nearly universal on paper but continuous only for the well-off. The coverage gap between subsidy eligibility and good insurance, plus Medicaid work-requirement churn, keeps millions cycling. Nobody knows what years of cycling do, and the 2029 Part D expansion will test whether public budgets absorb it.

Reward blunting is now a measured harm, an addiction treatment and a retail product at once. Growing numbers of lean people take low doses for calm and focus, with no trials in that population, often supplied by the same gray market behind the counterfeit harms.

Thinness has been commoditised and status has moved to muscle, premium agents and monthly dosing. If muscle-sparing combinations and MariTide stay expensive while generic semaglutide stays cheap, the body-as-income signal hardens into a two-tier pharmacology.

A class vision warning is attached to a drug a fifth of adults take, along with rising litigation and a 10-year pediatric registry that has barely begun. The safety picture is being written in real time on a population already committed.

prose.headline: Thin Got Cheap. Now Muscle Is What Money Looks Like.
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2028, about one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, and almost a third have tried one. Efficacy didn't drive most of that climb. Price did. Indian and Canadian generics made the American price look indefensible, and personal-import pens began arriving by mail at a fraction of the domestic cost. Then Novo Nordisk did what insulin makers once did: it launched its own unbranded semaglutide at fifty-nine dollars a month. Lilly cut its oral pill to seventy-nine. Brand exclusivity still runs into the early 2030s, but it no longer protects much.

Cheapness changed who pays. Employers were already retreating, and they took the fifty-nine-dollar sticker as permission to stop; fewer than half now cover weight management. The public sector went the other way. Medicare's bridge pilot was extended instead of being allowed to lapse. In December 2027 Congress lifted the decades-old ban on paying for weight-loss drugs under Part D, effective next year, after cheap semaglutide cut the budget score by more than half. Most Medicaid programs cover the unbranded pen. A federal grant makes it free at community health centres for uninsured adults under twice the poverty line, provided they sit through a nutrition visit. For most new starters, the government is now the payer.

The people left out sit between the lines. One is the home health aide whose employer dropped coverage. Another is the contractor earning just over the threshold. A third is the Medicaid enrollee who misses a work-requirement report and loses three months of coverage. For them the question is no longer whether the drug is affordable but whether this month is. That gap is where the gray market lives. In 2027 the CDC traced hundreds of emergency visits and two deaths to counterfeit pens, some filled with insulin. Customs seizures have multiplied, yet personal importation is still tolerated, a contradiction no one in Washington has resolved. The gray market's most reliable customers are people with no medical case for a prescription at all.

Those customers are the new part of the story. Telehealth brands now sell low-dose plans to lean people for calm, focus and freedom from craving, whether the craving is for snacks, wine, a phone or a cart. In late 2027 addiction-medicine guidelines endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder. The quieting that clinicians had logged as a side effect, and that a 2028 cohort finally measured, became a mechanism in one setting and a product in another. The FTC has warned three companies about their claims, and the category kept growing.

The safety picture is firmer and a little darker. Since February 2027 every GLP-1 drug carries a class warning for sudden optic-nerve vision loss. The absolute risk is small, but at this scale it means thousands of extra cases a year, and the lawsuits followed. Retatrutide arrived in spring 2028 with nearly thirty percent weight loss and a nerve-sensation warning. Amgen's monthly injection was approved in October and is only now reaching pharmacies, priced for the top tier.

The body has re-sorted itself. Anyone can be thin now, so thin means little. What fifty-nine dollars can't buy is muscle: the coach, the protein, the newer drugs that spare lean mass, and the continuity of never having to stop. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured, rural or deliberate. Snack volumes and spirits keep sliding, strength studios keep expanding, and restaurants serve half portions at full price. Some populists say the free shots are sedating the poor. No one has shown it, and the claim travels anyway. From the outside, nothing looks broken.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Ochoa sets two alarms. One is for work. The other is for the first Thursday of the month, when the pharmacy app releases the fifty-nine-dollar pens and they're gone by noon. This month she got them. Last month she didn't, and the pen she used instead came in a padded envelope, its carton printed in a script she couldn't read, and its dial clicked too easily.

At seven she is at Mr. Haskell's. He is eighty-one and on the Medicare one, and he has lost thirty pounds, much of it, she suspects, from his thighs. She spots him from bed to walker. He says he doesn't miss pie. He doesn't miss much, he adds, and she can't tell if that's a complaint.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap in the car. The other half goes back in the foil.

Yesenia, sixteen, texts a photo of a girl from school: shoulders, arms, the defined kind. No caption. Marisol knows what it means. That girl's mother has the good insurance and the gym with coaches. Yesenia wants to know about the new monthly shot. Marisol types back: it's twelve hundred dollars.

At home, Dario is on what his app calls a Quiet plan. It's a low dose he started for focus, though he was never heavy. He doesn't open a beer after work anymore, or argue about the Dodgers. He's easy to be around. She misses arguing.

Before bed she reads the leaflet, the boxed paragraph about sudden vision loss. Left eye closed, then right. The kitchen clock is sharp in both. She injects, caps the pen, and writes the date on the fridge calendar, where she writes everything that might run out.
